Age assurance sounds modest because age is only one fact. Yet proving that fact often requires another identifier (a government document, face scan, payment record, or account history). The website may not receive the raw evidence, but someone must process it. That intermediary becomes a gatekeeper—and the gatekeeper’s records may connect a person, a device, and a destination.

What happens when your child moves from a game to a health forum, a library resource, or a political discussion? If each service must distinguish adults from minors, the easiest operational answer may be a reusable credential. Companies won’t want to repeat expensive checks, and users can’t reasonably complete them at every door. A token designed to say “over eighteen” (or “under sixteen”) could gradually become the pass required to enter unrelated spaces.

That’s how a safety rule becomes infrastructure. The change doesn’t require a secret plan. It follows ordinary incentives: vendors seek more customers, platforms seek lower compliance costs, and agencies seek consistent enforcement. A credential accepted by one service becomes more valuable when accepted by many—then difficult to avoid once businesses build around it. The narrow checkpoint turns into a road system before the original rule expires.

Supporters may promise data minimization (collecting only what is necessary) or separation between the verifier and the website. Those protections matter, and lawmakers should write them clearly. But separation does not erase power. A verifier that repeatedly confirms age can still become a valuable vault of personal records, even if each participating site receives only a yes-or-no response. The map may be split among institutions while the roads still determine how services work.

The legal distinction also matters. A system may claim that it does not identify anyone because it returns only an age category. But persistent tokens, device signals, account recovery data, and transaction logs (the records needed to keep the service reliable) could permit linkage over time. Identity infrastructure isn’t merely a database containing names. It’s any durable system that sorts people, follows credentials, and controls access according to a stable relation.

Parents and privacy advocates are right to focus on children’s safety. We should also reject the false choice between protecting children and preserving private access to information. A protective measure should not quietly create routine identity checks for everyone. Lawmakers should require strict purpose limits (including bans on reuse), short retention periods, independent audits, and meaningful alternatives that do not demand identification. Agencies should not allow vendors to expand a safety credential into advertising, profiling, or general account registration.

The final test is practical, not rhetorical: Can a person use lawful online services without presenting a reusable identity signal? If the answer is no, the system has crossed the line—whatever the statute calls it. Demand that legislators define that line, prohibit crossing it, and impose consequences when companies do. When lawmakers describe online age checking as a narrow safety measure, parents should look past the label and examine the machinery. A rule aimed at one category of content may require every visitor to prove something about identity before speaking, reading, or browsing. The stated purpose may be limited (keeping minors from certain material), but the resulting system isn’t limited at all. It can become a general identity layer for online life.

Age assurance sounds modest because age is only one fact. Yet proving that fact often requires another identifier (a government document, face scan, payment record, or account history). The website may not receive the raw evidence, but someone must process it. That intermediary becomes a gatekeeper—and the gatekeeper’s records may connect a person, a device, and a destination.

What happens when your child moves from a game to a health forum, a library resource, or a political discussion? If each service must distinguish adults from minors, the easiest operational answer may be a reusable credential. Companies won’t want to repeat expensive checks, and users can’t reasonably complete them at every door. A token designed to say “over eighteen” (or “under sixteen”) could gradually become the pass required to enter unrelated spaces.

That’s how a safety rule becomes infrastructure. The change doesn’t require a secret plan. It follows ordinary incentives: vendors seek more customers, platforms seek lower compliance costs, and agencies seek consistent enforcement. A credential accepted by one service becomes more valuable when accepted by many—then difficult to avoid once businesses build around it. The narrow checkpoint turns into a road system before the original rule expires.

Supporters may promise data minimization (collecting only what is necessary) or separation between the verifier and the website. Those protections matter, and lawmakers should write them clearly. But separation does not erase power. A verifier that repeatedly confirms age can still become a valuable vault of personal records, even if each participating site receives only a yes-or-no response. The map may be split among institutions while the roads still determine how services work.

The legal distinction also matters. A system may claim that it does not identify anyone because it returns only an age category. But persistent tokens, device signals, account recovery data, and transaction logs (the records needed to keep the service reliable) could permit linkage over time. Identity infrastructure isn’t merely a database containing names. It’s any durable system that sorts people, follows credentials, and controls access according to a stable relation.

Parents and privacy advocates are right to focus on children’s safety. We should also reject the false choice between protecting children and preserving private access to information. A protective measure should not quietly create routine identity checks for everyone. Lawmakers should require strict purpose limits (including bans on reuse), short retention periods, independent audits, and meaningful alternatives that do not demand identification. Agencies should not allow vendors to expand a safety credential into advertising, profiling, or general account registration.

The final test is practical, not rhetorical: Can a person use lawful online services without presenting a reusable identity signal? If the answer is no, the system has crossed the line—whatever the statute calls it. Demand that legislators define that line, prohibit crossing it, and impose consequences when companies do. Children need safety, but families also need the freedom to seek information without building a permanent record of curiosity (and without asking an identity broker for permission). Protect both values at the architecture level, before convenience hardens into dependency.
